accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters (DfE, 2021) Literacy birth-to-three statements (enjoy sharing books with an adult; pay attention and respond to the pictures or the words; have favourite books and seek them out to share with an adult; repeat words and phrases from familiar stories) and the 3-4 statement on names of the parts of a book and page sequencing. The dialogic-reading description (prompt, evaluate, expand, repeat) follows Whitehurst et al. (1988) and the What Works Clearinghouse dialogic reading report. Nothing is claimed about letters or left-to-right tracking, which belong to 150 Understanding print.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the book-handling and sharing slips named in the adult text: starting from the back (scene 1 refuses Open it on the back cover, predict 1, p1, m5, challenge 'back'), holding it upside down (Open it refused while Duck is on his head, p3, challenge 'upside'), flicking many pages (the Flick button jumps and restarts at page 1, m1, challenge 'fast'), treating a wordless page as unshareable (predict 2 and the no-words park page, p5, challenge 'words'), a book read once being finished (predict 3, 'Put it away for good' refused, m2, challenge 'again') and rough hands (the pull card is refused, m8, challenge 'rough').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsharebook is built on physical book handling: a cover that flips between back and front and rotates 180 degrees, a two-page spread whose right-hand page is dragged leftwards to turn exactly one leaf (dragging the left page goes back, a flick skips and restarts), a wordless picture page answered by pointing, verb cards dragged onto animals, and a repeat-reading counter that grows the words the child joins in with. 150 Understanding print (flagprint) is about print direction and word gaps, 990 (flagpicstory) orders picture cards; lab shingle similarity is under 30% against every flag_*.js (lab_distinct gate passes).

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds each habit by trying it: Open it on the back cover says the front has the big picture and the name, opening upside down says turn it round, the page counter shows that single turns reach page 3 while a flick jumps away and restarts, the grown-up bubble asks 'Where is the dog?' on a page labelled 'no words on this page', a wrong verb drop names the cue ('its eyes are shut, it is sleeping') and each 'Again, please!' raises the joined-in words from 0 to 2, 4 and 6. The done messages confirm only after the action.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'At the back' (opening from the back is refused), 'No, we need words' (the no-words page is shared by pointing and the done message says so) and 'No, it is finished now' (each re-read lets the child say more words, shown by the counter).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions whose wrong options carry seven distinct slip messages: back (turn it over, the front has the picture and name), upside (turn the book round), fast (too many pages at once, we missed some), words (no words is fine, point and talk), again (a loved book can be read again and again), rough (gentle hands, pages can tear) and point (listen to the question, then point to that thing).

readability.evidence: Kid text is four short paragraphs of one- and two-syllable words (front, back, page, point, again) and passes the kid readability limit in validate_lessons; lab cards are one to five words with emoji pictures so a 2 to 3 year old can act with a grown-up reading; adult text uses the precise terms (shared reading, book handling, front cover, dialogic reading, expand) within the adult limit.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one book habit with its reason; the adult paragraphs give the curriculum placement, why talk and repeats matter (dialogic reading), the named mistakes with a keep-it-warm caution, and what the lab does. No content-gate filler phrase matches, and lab text is only instructions, the grown-up's questions and feedback.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px screenshots in light and dark: the cover and the round 'turn round' button sit side by side with the wide Open it card below, the two-page spread shows the page text and the turn-corner arrow, the four park circles are about 60 px across and do not overlap, the three verb cards and three animal cards fit in rows of three, and the three Again cards are full width. Young-mode buttons under the canvas are large; walk.cjs passed on iPhone 13 and desktop.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin (Turn it over, Turn it round, Open it, Turn one page, Go back one page, Flick lots of pages, Point to the dog/ball/duck/tree, pick a doing word then an animal, the three ask cards). The canvas aria-label is rewritten with each scene description and each piece of feedback, the challenge feedback is a role=status live region, right and wrong tiles carry ✓ / ✗ text as well as colour, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found nothing in light or dark on desktop and phone.

sources: Department for Education, Development Matters: non-statutory curriculum guidance for the EYFS (2021), Literacy: birth to three and 3 and 4-year-olds
Whitehurst, G. J. et al. (1988) Accelerating language development through picture book reading. Developmental Psychology 24(4), 552-559
What Works Clearinghouse (2007) Early Childhood Education intervention report: Dialogic Reading
BookTrust and National Literacy Trust (Words for Life) guidance on sharing books with babies and toddlers
